planting.note: Set container plants in spring or early fall into gritty, well-drained, neutral-to-acid soil; avoid root disturbance since daphnes resent transplanting once established.

directions: This slow-growing Himalayan species forms a dense, broad mound of small leathery leaves with a distinctive notched (retuse) tip, giving the plant its name. Clusters of fragrant rosy-pink to purplish flowers open at the branch tips in late spring, followed by small red berries later in the season. It prefers gritty, sharply drained soil and resents both waterlogging and summer drought, so even moisture without sogginess is the goal. Avoid disturbing the roots once sited, since established daphnes rarely transplant well.

planting.note: Plant in autumn while dormant-looking but about to leaf out, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered site with light shade.

directions: Native to Hokkaido and northern Honshu, this small deciduous-habit daphne follows an unusual seasonal rhythm: it leafs out in autumn, produces clusters of sweetly fragrant yellow flowers through the winter months, then drops its leaves and goes fully dormant over summer. Because it is actively growing and flowering during the coldest months, a sheltered woodland-edge position out of drying wind suits it best. Give it the same gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil favored by other alpine daphnes, and avoid summer watering once it has gone dormant. It remains uncommon in general cultivation but circulates through specialist alpine nurseries and rock-garden seed exchanges.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom.

directions: Collected in north-central China and named for the Italian missionary-botanist Giuseppe Giraldi, this wild forsythia is among the earliest of the genus to flower, opening pale primrose-yellow blossoms on bare arching branches ahead of most garden hybrids. Its lanky, fountain-like habit and somewhat sparser flower display compared to modern cultivars make it more of a botanical-interest and breeding-stock plant than a showy specimen shrub. Give it an open, sunny site with ordinary well-drained soil, and prune selectively right after flowering since, like all forsythias, it sets next year's buds on the current season's wood.

planting.note: Plant in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; its exceptional cold hardiness suits northern gardens where intermedia hybrids suffer bud loss.

directions: Native to the Manchuria-Korea border region, this is one of the hardiest forsythia species in cultivation, valued more for the flower-bud cold tolerance it has passed into breeding programs than for garden showiness on its own. It carries pale to mid-yellow flowers on a low, rounded, spreading frame in very early spring, flowering reliably even after harsh winters that damage less hardy relatives. It tolerates lean soils and exposed northern sites once established, and like other forsythias needs only post-bloom pruning to stay tidy. The named selection 'Vermont Sun' was developed from this species specifically for its bud hardiness.

planting.note: Plant in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; choose a site away from late-frost pockets since flowers open very early and can be nipped by a hard freeze.

directions: Native to Korea, this compact species is one of the most winter-hardy forsythias grown, with flower buds that survive temperatures that would kill those of the common intermedia hybrids. Rounded yellow blossoms open on bare stems earlier in spring than almost any other forsythia, a trait that made it a key hardiness donor for cold-climate cultivars such as 'Ottawa'. It stays smaller and denser than the roadside intermedia types, making it a better fit for foundation plantings in harsh-winter gardens. Prune immediately after flowering, since buds for the following year form on the current season's growth.

planting.note: Plant in early spring in well-drained, neutral-to-alkaline soil in full sun; this limestone-country native dislikes consistently wet feet.

directions: This is the only forsythia native to Europe, confined in the wild to a small limestone-mountain area of northern Albania, a striking outlier given that every other species in the genus comes from East Asia. It carries pale yellow flowers on slender arching stems in early spring, generally smaller and less densely borne than the Asian hybrids sold as garden shrubs. Its limestone origin means it prefers lean, sharply drained, neutral-to-alkaline soil and resents heavy wet clay. It remains a botanical curiosity rather than a common landscape plant, found mainly through botanic garden collections and specialist or rock-garden seed exchanges.
